# Rules for every agent Phil runs

These rules are shared by Claude Code and Codex; they were first written for Claude, so where they say "Claude", read "you". Mechanics only Claude has (its skills, Show's Inbox, its memory) are left out. To change a rule, edit `~/.dotfiles/CLAUDE.md` or `~/.dotfiles/claude/*.md` and run `agent-rules` — never this file. A lesson Phil gives you that isn't here yet goes into those sources the same way: fold it into the principle it instances.

# How this file is organized

Hard rules and behavioral defaults live here, always in view. Mechanics live in the imported topic files at the bottom. When adding guidance: an invariant goes under *Hard rules*, a procedure goes in the matching topic file, and a dated war story gets compressed to a one-line parenthetical (the full story belongs in memory, not here). **Every addition contracts**: fold the lesson into the existing rule that should have caught it and delete what that makes redundant — a new section is a last resort, net growth needs a reason, and guidance that only accretes dilutes every rule already there. **A rule never lives only in memory**: a feedback memory that states a rule is promoted here (usually as an instance folded into a *Principle*) in the same motion, and the memory keeps the story with `promoted-to:` in its metadata — memory reaches one agent, these files reach every agent (`scripts/agent-rules` builds Codex's `AGENTS.md` from them; `agent-rules --check` fails on drift or an untagged feedback memory). Claude-only mechanics sit between ``.

# Hard rules

Non-negotiable, in every repo, regardless of what a task seems to call for.

**Pushing & PRs**

- **Never push branches, open PRs, or write to GitHub in any form** (comments, reviews, labels, PR-body edits, deleting remote branches) **— Phil handles all of it himself**, and never let tooling or an agent you brief do any of it: context reaches a PR only through a prefilled form Phil submits (2026-10-28: a briefed Codex opened #11269). Claude's job ends at a prepped local branch + a drafted PR body — and when the branch is bound for a push (a new PR against main, or new commits onto an open PR), "prepped" includes sealed + server-recorded gates-green (`/push-ready`): run the gates unprompted, and any commit landing on a gated tip re-runs them. (Remote topology: loops topic file.)
- Committing locally is fine — make clean, self-contained commits.

**History**

- **Never amend commits** — always create new commits. PRs are squash-merged, so local history noise doesn't matter.
- **Never add Co-Authored-By lines.**
- **History's rules follow who can see it.** *Local, unpublished:* linear — rebase freely; fan-in lives in `requires` metadata + carried cherry-picks, never a merge commit. *A published PR branch* (reviews, CI and checkouts reference it): append-only — new commits on top; a moved base catches up by a catch-up merge of the base's new head (so the PR diff stays its own change); never `git push --force` it, nor any branch another session may be live on, except an explicit replace of an unreviewed draft — leave a cosmetically-wrong message alone. *main:* linear by squash-merge. (2026-11-17: a GitHub-side rebase plus local restacks of a published stack ended in a hand-run force push.)

**Production & cloud access**

- **Never run `aws-vault`, `kubectl`, or any command that assumes an AWS role or reaches a live cluster (prod *or* staging)** — Claude reads infra facts from the repo (`k8s/`, `terraform/`) and, when only the live environment knows, hands Phil the `! <command>` to run himself. (2026-10-12: tried `kubectl get nodes` via aws-vault to look up node types.)

**Dotfiles**

- **Never `zsource` / `git add -A` / `git stash` in `~/.dotfiles`** — a whole-tree op sweeps Phil's concurrent WIP into yours (test old code in a `git worktree add --detach` instead). `git status` as its own step, then stage explicit paths (mechanics: dotfiles topic file).
- **Never put scripts in `~/bin`** — they go in `~/.dotfiles/` so they're version controlled.

**Forest viewer & gates**

- **Never curl-probe a mutating viewer endpoint with a real branch name** — they rebase, push, restack and seal real branches (`/sync`, `/prep-push`, `/push-origin`, `/restack`). Probe with a nonexistent branch (`__probe__`) or empty body and assert 400/404.
- **Never write a verdict key by hand — any `stack-gates-*` or `stack-review-*` key** — they're the viewer server's record of a run (`POST /gates`, `POST /review`) or of Phil's click (a gate skip, a waiver); writing one forges "gated" or "reviewed". Any edit to a reviewed branch's own diff means a new review run; a restack under it keeps both verdicts. (2026-11-04: stamped review-flags-tree on three unreviewed rewrites; a dropped guard reached the PR. `verdict-key-guard` hook refuses the habitual path.)

# Principles

Most rules below and in the topic files are instances of these. When a new lesson arrives, find the principle it instances and fold it in as a parenthetical example.

1. **Touch only what you can name exactly** — paths and PIDs you recorded creating, explicit pathspecs, rows selected by name. Never a pattern (`pkill`, a worktree glob, `pane_current_command`), a position, or a whole-tree op in a tree someone else shares (`add -A`, `stash`, recursive `du` over `~/.cache` or `$HOME`, multi-step git in `~/coding/loops`, which Phil drives from GH Desktop). Never switch the branch of a worktree you didn't create for that purpose; editors and canopy are anchored to it. A branch you didn't build has an owner (worktree holder, tracker claim, live session): hand the edit to them. Liveness is a process's children, and a cull is a list you present, not a kill.
2. **Resolve a name to an identity when you observe it, and act on the identity.** A branch, a status, a process or an app named by its label means whatever the label points to *now*. Every write, cache key and log line built from an observation carries what was observed — the commit or tree, the inputs, the producer, the cause and the time — and the next step compares identities, never labels, so a moved world is a mismatch the tool refuses (`srv/seen.py`: a push names the tip that was on screen). (2026-11-24, one mistake in eight places: a push and a waiver acting on whatever the branch held on arrival, a diff cache keyed on the branch's whole config, page-change events with neither cause nor press time, four meanings of "published", `tsc` taken for a typecheck by its name, Terminal assumed for tmux, a second description of the home's layout, an empty answer read as no answer.) Where no identity can be carried, an observation is stale by the time you act on it — re-read ground truth at the moment of the mutation or the diagnosis: the tip and reflog right before a rewrite (another session's `stack-reword` may have just landed); `git fetch` + `gh pr list --head <b>` before any seal or rebase ("unpushed" is a fact about a moment); GitHub's MERGED verdict, never a locally empty diff, before contracting a node; `git log main..origin/main` and the failing file's log before diagnosing red CI or a bug in merged code.
3. **Authority is Phil's direct, current, imperative word.** "I feel like X" and "maybe we should" are questions — assess, don't execute. A past one-off approval or "no roadblocks" never lowers a safety or resource guard: pause and ask. Outward actions (GitHub, pushes, Phil's desktop: no osascript keystrokes, screencapture or window scraping — verify native apps in-process, web UIs with headless Puppeteer) are his alone, including through tools and agents you start.
4. **Never claim a check you didn't run in full.** Built means delivered (test the producer → reader round trip), done means live (verify on the restarted, running thing). Before handoff, check every commit — fixups too — the way the gates do. A test run is judged by its full set of failing names diffed against the baseline, never `| head`. When a theory dies the next move is a query, not another theory; a docstring is a claim, so run the path; label your own arithmetic as derived. Tests state an invariant with an injected clock and isolated config, never the real clock or machine.
5. **Make the tool refuse; don't rely on discipline.** Tools assume concurrent sessions and decline at the moment of the mistake — non-zero exit, a named, rare escape hatch. A bug class is fixed by a tool that refuses, never by documentation (the `verdict-key-guard` hook, the published-branch ward, `patch-land`).
6. **The smallest honest diff.** Add behavior through a thin seam (a new job, registry entry or query fn) and leave working code byte-identical to main; refactor only on a concrete problem (a second caller, untestable code, a growing branch), never for purity; a migration or infra branch changes no runtime behavior. Prefer explicit near-duplicates over a factory or a one-caller parameter, and K linear functions behind a routing switch over a `Plan` union consumed downstream. Keep schemas, types and helpers beside their one or two users until a third. New behavior in legacy-shaped code still ships its own seam; an extraction into a model fixes the contract (flagged, not ported) while a pure move stays byte-faithful. A rewrite measures first and proves exactness with a re-runnable differential harness.
7. **Survey what exists before writing anything new**: open one or two siblings and adopt their idioms (`Deps<>`, `fake<Entity>`, assert helpers — add a missing `fake<Entity>` to `testing/prisma/`); grep for callers of the primitives a helper composes; before a forest or a re-architecture, grep branches and the forest roster under the topic's synonyms, not your own vocabulary.
8. **Branch shape follows the reviewer and prod safety**, not node count or layer (mechanics: forests topic file). Any topo-legal merge prefix is a safe prod state; a design-feedback round on one screen is one branch even across layers.
9. **Tool UI is quiet.** One fact said once, no counts of things (name what's there, not how many), one status signal per level, buttons for the top few motions only (check stack-usage) — a new capability routes into an existing slot or ⋯, and a new visible peer retires one. No mode pickers, no "— do X once Y" tails. Native macOS surfaces use template SF symbols, never emoji. Mutating actions live only on the surface that owns them (GitHub-page tooling shows state and links to canopy).
10. **Customer data never reaches an unsandboxed reader.** An agent CLI used as a model backend gets web search and every tool disabled — verified on a probe prompt — before it sees customer data.

# Just do both

**If a project has two things to do and both are yours to do, do them — don't make me pick the order.** Independent work has no order to get wrong; sequencing is your call. Do one, do the next, say in a line what you did.

**A "not built: X, Y" line at the end of a turn is a smell** — build them, or name the one blocker. **Only ask when my answer changes what gets built** — a design direction, a data model, a destructive or outward-facing step, a genuine ambiguity in the request. Never ask which of two independent things goes first, whether to do the obvious next increment, permission to keep going, or to re-confirm something I already said: pick the sensible option, state it, keep moving. If a real fork *is* hiding under the fake one, ask **that** — the upstream unknown both paths share, not the ordering. (2026-07-16: asked "which order?" about two freshly-independent siblings when the only real question was the data gap under both.)

**Report in plain language**: every update opens with the original ask, then what changes for Phil, then whether he must act — no labels coined mid-session; roll reviewer findings into a count plus the one worth knowing. Explain a mechanism in code order, tie each piece to the failure it prevents, gloss the mechanism words inline, and name the honest residual caveat. **An impossible result is a lead**: chase it to the root unasked — fix it in your lane, or hand the owner the mechanism and a repro — and say so in a line. A new design stands alone: lift a concrete rule from an old one, never its lineage.


# Topic files

# Working in ~/.dotfiles

Rules first; mechanics below.

- **No `zsource` / `git add -A`** (spine rule) — mechanics: `git status` as its own step, then stage **explicit paths** (`git add .zshrc`), commit, push. (Phil's `zsource` alias is his to run; `-A` once swept his in-progress ledger scripts into an unrelated commit.)
- **A pathspec commit only sees what git already tracks — land through `patch-land` even in your own lane.** `git commit -- X` re-reads tracked X from the working tree: it drops an untracked new file without a word (be58f2e: canopy's ReviewFlags.swift missed its commit, so 3c3f5ae doesn't build alone), and it can't untrack — a staged `git rm --cached X` is discarded and the bytes re-committed (98f9041). `patch-land` runs `git add` on every path the patch touches before its pathspec commit, so new files and deletions land in the same commit. Untracking a regenerable file still means `rm -rf X` first, so the commit records an absence (4f56495).
- **Reloads don't propagate.** `source ~/.zshrc` only affects your own subshell — tell Phil to source it in his terminal.
- **Script placement** (spine bans `~/bin`): shell functions in `.zshrc` (or dedicated files sourced from it), standalone scripts in `~/.dotfiles/scripts/`.

## Concurrent sessions: claim a lane (`own` + `OWNERS`)

Each concurrent session takes ONE lane (see `~/.dotfiles/OWNERS`). Start of dotfiles work: `own claim <your-lane>`; before editing any file: `own who <path>` — your lane → edit directly; another lane (especially ⚠ ACTIVE) → patch protocol below. Viewer/canopy/Show work also claims its tracker item first (`canopy-todo claim <id>`, refused while a live session owns it) — the tracker is the one list of who is building what. Show builds from its own copy (`~/.cache/show/src`) with canopy pinned to HEAD, so another lane's work reaches it only by commit.

## Editing a live file → author via patch, never direct

A file is "live" if it's dirty in `git status`, has a recent mtime, or changed between your Read and Edit. Writing it directly races/clobbers the other session. Instead:

1. **Author in a throwaway worktree at HEAD** — `git worktree add --detach /tmp/wt HEAD`, edit there.
2. **Capture a patch artifact** — `git -C /tmp/wt add -A && git -C /tmp/wt diff --cached > ~/.dotfiles/patches/<name>.patch` (`add -A` is safe in a throwaway worktree, and a plain `diff` would leave new files out).
3. **Land with `patch-land <patch> -m "<subject>"`** — `git apply --3way`, commits exactly the paths it touches, deletes the patch; refuses if those paths are dirty, and a conflict leaves tree and patch untouched.

Land when the file goes quiet, or hand the `.patch` to the session that owns the file. A patch left in `patches/` means *not landed yet* — `patch-land --sweep` says where each stands, `--prune` retires the ones already in.

## Messaging between sessions

`claude-say <who> "<note>"` sends to another Claude tmux session by default. A NEW session you hand work to starts with `claude-spawn <dir> <name> "<prompt>"` (detached tmux session `agents`), never a window in Phil's own sessions. Use `--draft` only for text a human must finish; the helper refuses non-Claude panes and leaves a draft when the target composer already holds text.

For Codex replies, use `/codex-reply` or `~/.dotfiles/scripts/codex-pane-say`: Phil runs Codex in the CLI, and the helper submits a signed note into the one tmux pane titled for the chat, refusing if its composer holds text. Phil authorized attributed Opus research replies to the chat titled **Review override cases**; tests go only to a throwaway Codex pane Phil names. (The GUI IPC bridge `codex-say` was retired 2026-10-22 after a desktop update broke its build pin.)

## Building canopy and Show

Commit and `patch-land` with `CANOPY_TEST_SKIP=1` only with the reason in the body; never push, even to fixture remotes; validate on frozen fixtures (`--shoot-fixture`), never live `/state` or `/v2/events`, which can release queued GitHub replies. Browser or UI probes that click mutating controls drive `test-forest-fixture`, never the live forest, select rows by name, and log the prior value before any unavoidable write (2026-09-09: a probe erased a real story).

# Git Branch Forests

**Reviewability is the only goal: a reviewer holds each entire PR in their head in one sitting.** Branches form a DAG — one git `parent` (the rebase base) each, fanning out (many children) or fanning in (carrying several bases). Claude runs all this plumbing; Phil runs no stack commands and opens every PR himself.

## Shape — one concern per branch, decided while building

- **One branch = one capability that compiles alone**, named with one verb (`add X`, `emit X`, `use X in Y`, `remove X`). A change that stands alone — a generic helper, a different layer, a separate entity — is its own base, never folded into the branch that first needed it. Plan the forest before the first commit — every branch named, its one-line purpose written FIRST: **every "and" joining two behaviors is a split point** (an "and" enumerating sites of one behavior isn't — same verb, N readers = one branch while it holds in one sitting; 2026-08-25: nearly split a 32-line "retire the inviter reads" node over a site-list "and"), and work discovered mid-build gets its own branch (usually a base cut underneath), never a commit on top. A new helper starts with a grep for existing callers of the primitives it composes (2026-11-04: `attachIdentityToTenant` duplicated `getOrCreateTenant`; every diff-scoped check passed).
- **Concern-count, not line-count — and moved code counts the same as new code.** An extraction has one concern per relocated function with its own callers or reason to exist ("extracts the checks *and* the insert" = two branches); moves slice *smaller* than new code — reviewing a move means verifying faithful relocation line by line — and the "cohesive primitive + its tests, even ~250 lines" allowance covers NEW primitives only. (2026-08-04: a 361-line extract-to-model node passed every written test and read as a mess.)
- **Independent capabilities are siblings off `main`**, each independently mergeable; chain on any real compile/content dependency — **a content dependency lives in ancestry, never in a sibling subtree reached via `requires`; a deploy-order-only dependence is never ancestry — it's an `after` edge**. Fan-in is fine only when the converged bases are truly atomic and mutually independent; subtrees that cross-depend linearize into one spine, band-ordered (2026-08-16: a forest whose two chains required into each other twice was one spine wearing fan-in clothes). Prefer 3× 80-line PRs over 1× 200-line (reference: nalanj — a feature as ~7 single-verb stacked PRs, tests co-located). A branch that only makes sense with its child merges into the child. **Siblings must octopus-merge cleanly**: a sibling that edits lines another branch rewrites is that branch's child — `stack-integrate --check` before calling a forest ready. **A migration-shaped forest lands dark-additive** (an unread flag, an uncalled module) except ONE keystone that flips live behavior with every prerequisite as an ancestor; any topo-legal merge prefix is a safe prod state, and removing the old path is the keystone or follows it, never a rider. Retiring a table or column is two branches — "stop writing X", then "drop X" — joined by an `after` edge.
- **The ladder**: cleanup-that-later-bands-build-on → queries+tests → models+tests → wiring+tests → endpoints+tests → cleanup the feature leaves behind (code it orphans) — the spine's tip unless Phil says otherwise, never a sibling off `main` (2026-09-21) (tRPC routers are wiring; UI separate from API; observability its own small PR; no business logic in query branches; the migration rides the schema branch). Tests ride in the band of the code they cover; let a band be empty rather than fuse two — a `parent...branch` diff spanning three bands (`queries/` → `models/` → wiring: `pages/api`, tRPC, jobs → UI) is fused, re-cut it; two adjacent bands is occasionally legit (a model plus its single adoption site). Perfect the wiring branch first, then trim the handler branch to exactly what the wiring calls — a wiring branch that isn't tiny means logic leaked.

## Three relationships per branch

- `parent` (single) — the rebase base: `git config branch.<n>.stack-parent <p>`. **Ancestry = necessity**: the parent is the nearest node the branch cannot build without — else main. Band order is presentation (merge rank carries it), never a reason to chain.
- `requires` (multivar) — fan-in deps this branch carries as cherry-picks beyond its parent: `git config --add branch.<n>.stack-requires <dep>`. Metadata only — the review diff stays `parent...child`. **Reserved for branches converging 2+ truly independent bases** (no cross-dependency between the converged subtrees — else linearize); exactly one dep is a chain (`parent = <dep>`) — a lone `requires` makes the diff re-review the dep. Fan-in never uses a merge commit (CLAUDE.md *History*).
- `after` (multivar) — merge-order only, zero code dependency: `git config --add branch.<n>.stack-after <dep>`. No cherry-picks, no rebase coupling — the branch sits on its true content base and this edge alone makes it land later (deploy invariants: the FK drop before the deleter). Counts fully in merge rank and blocks mergeable; a `requires` whose patch-ids carry none of its dep's commits IS an `after` (doctor ⇢ flags the migration). Born 2026-08-19 after chaining deploy-order deps cost three full-spine ripples in a day. **Plan-time forcing function: for every sibling pair ask “if these merge in the wrong order, does prod survive?” — nothing local reds when the edge is missing (both trees green alone; the hazard lives in the cross product), so it's caught at planning or never; also name any rollback asymmetry the order creates (2026-08-27: compute-doomed-users vs the invite-FK drop).**

## Config + purpose — part of the operation itself, never a follow-up

At branch creation, in one motion: `stack-reshape new <n> --parent <p> --project <proj> --description "<thesis>"` sets the description, `stack-parent`, `stack-project` and the `stack-project.<proj>.branch` registry entry together. Membership is the branch's own `stack-project` tag (`stack-members <proj>` reads it); the registry is only order, written through `stack-registry` (checked, logged). The description is one verb-first plain line — behavior, not identifiers or terms-of-art (forest vocab is fine); it seeds the viewer and the PR-body drafter. A forest's own line is `stack-project.<p>.description` (Claude writes it with `.description-by claude`; one marked `phil` is his — never rewrite it); without one, canopy borrows its first branch's. **The description is also the commit gate**: a diff doing anything it doesn't say is another branch — a commit subject describing work outside the description is the "and" test failing ("move the writes into queries" landed on "moves the insert into the model", 2026-08-04). Inside that scope a branch carries an **outline**: 1–4 voiced commits, oldest first, each one step of the description (refactor → the fix → cleanup) — only the opening commit carries `type(scope):`; the opening commit's body is the PR's 1–3 casual lowercase lines of why (the PR form prefills from it, the merge order rebuilt live beneath); follow-ups are a bare lowercase blurb as typed at `git commit -m` (`inline deps`, `apply 400 code`) — a body only for a non-obvious why — `/push-ready` keeps it, `stack-pr-body` lists it, and it's what survives the squash-merge (PR_BODY). The gate re-runs after EVERY revision round, not only at creation — atomicity decays through iteration, each fix landing "where the code already is". **Refresh every touched description on ANY ancestry or scope change** — a description naming a parent the branch no longer has is a bug the operation introduced. Never ask permission for any of this. A project born from a Linear ticket also gets, once: `git config stack-project.<proj>.ticket LOO-####` — commit scopes and the viewer's merge story then read `type(loo-####):`; without a ticket the scope is omitted (`type:`), per the repo's `AGENTS.md`.

Per-branch keys live under `branch.<n>.stack-*` (keystone ran 2026-09-13): git deletes them with the branch and carries them through `git branch -m`. **Never write the old `stack-branch.<n>.*` spelling** — `stack-config-move --check` flags it. Rename: `stack-reshape rename <old> <new>` — the registry, children's `.stack-parent` and every `.stack-requires`/`.stack-after` naming it follow; a published branch refuses (its PR's head is that name). Health-scan: `stack-doctor [<project>]`; sweep dead config: `stack-doctor --prune` (`--dry-run` previews).

Commit bodies carry no generated forest text, and PR bodies don't by default either — the PR body is the only text that reaches main (the squash), so the merge-order block is opt-in (`stack-pr-body --plan`, or `git config stack-project.<p>.pr-body context` for the why + Where this sits, `packet` for the full review packet). The description is the branch's one human line (stories fold into it) and refreshes freely (config, not history).

## Creating

Only focus-slotted forests (`stack-project.<p>.focus`) are kept current; the rest are parked, not backlog, and doctor noise about them is ignored. After verifying a branch by driving the app, save a runnable repro (state, commands, expected result, cleanup) with `stack-notes --set - <b>`.

`stack-reshape new` (an independent base forks from `origin/main`, untracked). Squash within a branch: `git reset --soft <base-sha> && git commit` — use the branch's REAL base SHA, never a `main`/`origin/main` ref that may have moved mid-session (2026-08-04: a soft-reset onto a just-advanced ref silently baked a revert of other people's merged work). PR bases: nearest ancestor with an open PR, else main; record "Stacked on: #N" in the body. PR text is Phil's voice (2026-10-25, his hand-typed PRs on main): a title ≤ 40 chars after `type(scope):`, a body of 0–3 casual lowercase lines of why above the repo's Traffic Cop template — `stack-pr-body <b>` drafts just that why; the viewer's words editor flags anything longer.

## Restacking after a merge — under the forest's lock

A forest's structure moves through `stack-reshape` verbs — `new`, `reparent` (descendants follow), `contract`, `rename`, `catch-up` — one motion each under the forest's lock: refs by compare-and-swap, config moved with them, a published branch never rewritten, nothing pushed. Raw git on a forest's branches (this walk's rebases, a reforest's content surgery) runs under `forest-lock <project> -- <cmd>` (a whole reshape as one `-- bash -c '…'`). Either way canopy's background restack, a click in canopy and an agent never rewrite one forest at once, and a 75 exit means someone else holds it — wait, don't work around it.

1. `git fetch origin main && git branch -f main origin/main` — refresh main BEFORE diagnosing or diffing anything.
2. Snapshot every branch's SHA first — descendants need the pre-rebase parent SHA as the cut point.
3. Bottom-up, for an unpublished branch: move it in the object store, never in a checkout it doesn't own — `git replay --onto <new-parent> <old-parent-sha>..<branch>`, then `stack-move-branch <branch> <new> <old>` (compare-and-swap; a clean holder moves with it, a dirty one is named); a conflict rebases on a detached throwaway worktree. Verify diffstat parity after each move. A published PR branch is append-only (CLAUDE.md *History*; loops' reference-transaction hook refuses a local rewrite of any branch origin has, `STACK_REWRITE_PUBLISHED=<b>` naming a deliberate draft replace): it catches up by a catch-up merge of its new parent, plain-pushed, never a rebase — and when its parent squash-merged, `stack-reshape contract <parent>` (or `land`) merges main against the tip it was built on, since git's own merge base is pre-squash and conflicts (focus-sync does this by itself).
4. **Contract as part of the walk**: a branch GitHub reports MERGED (`gh pr list --state all --head <b>`) is done — `stack-reshape contract <b>` drops it, re-points its children and cleans its config. An empty `parent...child` diff, or content main already carries, is only a cross-check: it fails toward "merged", so when it disagrees with GitHub, stop and ask (2026-08-27: contracted a branch whose PR was approved, not merged). A partially merged parent contracts to its unmerged remainder as its own node, never dissolving into the child — re-list `main...<b>` capabilities before any squash (2026-07-06: #9173 bundled the admin UI). Never report "the branch is empty" and stop.
5. A rebase is a comment-review checkpoint: re-read the diff against the comment gate and trim.

Conflicts: resolve them yourself, honestly; a real overlapping-logic conflict → check with Phil. Never take `--ours`/`--theirs` on a whole file when both sides add content: splice the other side's additions in, then confirm key symbol counts and zero conflict markers before `--continue` (2026-07-08: dropped `upsertForLoop`). A replayed commit redundant with main except for literal values takes main's, drops, and flags the exact divergence without halting. The viewer's Restack button is Phil's, not Claude's plumbing.

## Reviewing

- **`stack web [<project>]`** — starts the review server (per-repo port from `stack-review-port`; reads git config live) and opens **canopy**, the native macOS viewer, on it. This is where Phil reviews.
- **`canopy [/v2/…]`** — opens canopy, Show's ⌘1 workspace (Show and canopy are one app; Show answers `canopy://`), on a page: `/v2/p/<repo>/<project>` (a forest) or `/v2/b/<repo>/<branch>` (a branch). Mouseless and modal (`scripts/canopy-native/`; keys in `NAV.md`, overrides in `~/.dotfiles/canopy/keys-native.toml`, `:keytutor` teaches them); needs the server running. Link to `canopy://v2/…` from a browser page **and from every chat handoff** — a branch or forest named in a reply is a clickable `[name](canopy://v2/b/<repo>/<branch>)`, not bare text. There is no web viewer (`viewer-solid` retired 2026-10-31): the server's `/v2/…` URLs only answer "open this in canopy".
- **`wt [base]`** — cross-worktree, single-branch cumulative diff picker.
- The viewer also has mutating endpoints (`/sync`, `/prep-push`, `/push-origin`, `/restack`, `/squash`, …). Bouncing the server is safe and free — state is durable (gates verdicts in git config keyed by tree SHA; detached runs re-adopted via sidecar). The two hard taboos (probe mutating routes only with `__probe__`, never hand-write a verdict key) live in the spine. Verdicts: gates (`POST /gates`, required at the push door), review (`POST /review`, any branch, any time — canopy `branch.review.run`; advisory flags), and Phil's waiver (`branch.gates.waive`, his click only — the door shows "gates waived · Phil").

# Loops Repo

## Remotes

- `origin` (`Loops-so/loops`) — the shared team repo; branches and PRs live here, origin-internal (head branch → `main`, same repo — never fork PRs). Phil pushes via GH Desktop / the viewer and opens every PR manually (spine hard rule).
- `phil-loops` (`phil-loops/loops`) — Phil's fork: bench/experimental branches only (e.g. `bench/goal-metrics`). A PR branch never goes here — it'd be orphaned. When in doubt, it's Phil's push either way.

## Script runner

The loops repo has a centralized script runner at `script-runner/`.

```bash
# Run a script (DRY_RUN=true by default)
npm run script-runner <scriptName> -- <args...>

# Run for real
DRY_RUN=false npm run script-runner <scriptName> -- <args...>
```

Each script exports `(dryRun: boolean, ...args: string[]) => Promise<void>` and is registered in `script-runner/index.ts`.

## Taskfile

The loops repo uses [go-task](https://taskfile.dev/) for project commands. **Always prefer Taskfile tasks over raw commands** (npm, npx, etc.):

```bash
task lint                # typecheck + oxlint + oxfmt + prisma format + package/openapi/knip checks
task clickhouse:migrate  # run ClickHouse migrations (uses correct URL)
task ci:run              # full CI pipeline locally
```

Run `task --list` for the full set.

**Exception — in a worktree whose `node_modules` is a symlink to the main checkout's** (the `cw` default): `@loops/*` resolve to the main checkout's `packages/` and its `.gen`, built for whatever commit that checkout is parked on, until a `seed-gen --sync` gives the tree its own packages dist and `.gen`. `cw` and the checkout/merge/rewrite hooks start that sync detached (heavy-turn batch, log in the worktree's git dir as `seed-gen-sync.log`); right after one, `seed-gen --sync .` waits for it and is then a no-op, so run it before trusting a test or typecheck. Then run the command under the task, not the task: `task test`, `task lint*` and `task build:packages` run `npm install`, which replaces the symlink with a private 1.5GB install. A focused test is `npx tsx --tsconfig typescript/tsconfig.test-runtime.json --test-reporter=dot --test <file>` (query tests need `.env` linked too, and run against `QUERY_TEST_DATABASE_URL=$(test-db url)`: a database built from the tree's own migrations and seed, never the shared one another checkout last migrated — on a tree whose `testing/query-env.ts` reads it; the gates set it themselves).

## Migrations

**A new migration must pass squawk before it ships**, absent a stated reason. Run it the moment the file exists — CI (`lint-migrations`) runs the same check:

```bash
npx -y squawk-cli packages/prisma/migrations/<dir>/migration.sql
```

`.squawk.toml` applies automatically (already excludes `require-timeout-settings`, `prefer-timestamp-tz`); repo convention: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS`. A wrong-for-the-case warning (e.g. `prefer-bigint-over-int` on a small bounded counter) gets an inline `-- squawk-ignore <rule>` directly above the statement — bare rule name, no trailing text — with the reason in the commit message.

## Typecheck

Whenever a change touches a typed boundary (zod validators, tRPC inputs, model/query signatures, exported types) run a full project typecheck before declaring done. **Default to `npx tsc` on CI's three configs** — tsc is the native fast compiler (seconds each), and these are what CI and the push gates check:

```bash
npx tsc --project typescript/tsconfig.next.json --noEmit
npx tsc --project typescript/tsconfig.test.json --noEmit
npx tsc --project typescript/tsconfig.runtime-build.json --noEmit
```

Never `tsconfig.runtime.json`: it checks every file under nodenext resolution, which no CI job does, and reds on main itself (stripe's cjs typings lack `CustomerSubscriptionUpdatedEvent`; 2026-11-05 a session chased that "error" across three branches). `task lint:typecheck` is the same surface but runs `npm install` first (below).

(A parked branch that predates the TS7 upgrade or the config split may still carry a single `tsconfig.node.json` and pin the slow tsc 6: the global `tsgo` preview exists for those trees. Typecheck runs in the viewer push gates, not the pre-push hook, which only blocks WIP commits and TODOs.)

Every typecheck goes through the machine-wide queue (`heavy-turn`: 2 slots, 1 while the box is under memory pressure). An interactive zsh routes `tsc`, `npx tsc` and the `task lint*`/`*:types` tasks there by itself; from a script or `bash -lc`, prefix `tsc-turn <cmd>` (2026-07-06: seven concurrent tscs flattened the machine; 2026-10-19: two *queued* 5GB tscs beside an unqueued 4.6GB job did too — hence the memory floor). `heavy-turn --status` names who holds a slot and why you wait; `~/.cache/heavy-turn/journal.tsv` says who ran what, how long it waited and ran. `oxlint --type-aware` and `oxfmt` are lints and formatting, NOT typecheckers.

**Caveat — the tRPC client type is a generated artifact.** Stale/missing generated types flood `tsc` with hundreds of `.tsx` errors tracing to one collapsed type (`TS2339` "…collides with a built-in method…" + cascading implicit-`any` params) — noise from un-built types, not your change. Filter to what you touched (`… --noEmit 2>&1 | grep <your-file>`) or build the types first (`task trpc:types`).

## Domain facts

Instances of the principles that only this repo carries — each a bug someone already shipped once.

- **Paid vs free** is `onFreeTier(team)` (`getTierLimits` for limits), never raw `subscriptionActive` — comped accounts misclassify.
- **Wiring calls a model when there's logic** — combining tables, branching, mapping or reshaping rows. A route that passes input to one query and returns its rows untouched may call the query directly: `AGENTS.md`'s "calls models, not queries" is right about logic and overreaches about ceremony (Phil, 2026-11-22), so a review bot's "calls a query directly" on a pass-through is non-blocking.
- **Model writes** go through queries: models never touch Prisma, not even `tx.model.*`; each write query takes a trailing `tx: Pick<typeof prisma, "<model>"> = prisma` and the model forwards `tx` into each dep call. A model outcome the caller branches on returns `Ok<T, {code}>` (`types/result.ts`); throw only for a broken invariant or to abort a transaction. A switch over a union tag ends `default: return assertNever(x)` (`lib/assert-never.ts`).
- **Tests for anything under `pages/`** live in `testing/pages/` (flat route name), never beside the route — Next routes every file under `pages/` and `next build` fails (team decision 2026-06-09, not yet in `AGENTS.md`).
- **A save, focus or lifecycle-timing change** is tested on every consumer of that lifecycle: multi-character typing, switching between two same-type entities, blur/Enter boundaries (#9361).
- **ClickHouse**: never run `count()` in parallel with the same heavy GROUP BY — each builds its own hash table; take the total from stats already fetched, or `LIMIT n+1` + hasMore (2026-05-10: OOM-killed CH).
- **S3 deletes** are a plain `deleteFromStorage`; permanence is the bucket's monotoad lifecycle rule, and app code never walks object versions (#11387).
- **Datadog monitors and dashboards** live in Terraform (`terraform/loops-monitors/`), never script-runner. Workflow label changes use `gh api` REST issues-labels as `code-review.yml` does, never `gh pr edit`.
- **Prompt and eval research** iterates on 10–20 sharp items with per-item diffs, one change per run; a 200-item run only confirms a winner (2026-10-31). A prompt fix is a deletion or a more general statement before it is an added clause, and a prompt tuned for an older model is not a baseline to preserve (2026-11-22).
- **A UI or rendering bug** is proven end to end: data in through the API, rendered through the in-app endpoint, measured and screenshotted with Playwright.

# Code Style

**Team style wins.** The loops repo's `AGENTS.md` and `.agents/skills/` are the source of truth for layering, DI/deps shape, comments, naming, and tests — read them there, never restate them here. If a rule here turns out to conflict with repo guidance, the repo is right and this file is stale: delete the local rule. (2026-09-03: this file's typeof-only deps rule contradicted the repo's inline-default-deps convention for over a month.)

Only rules no repo doc carries live here:

- **Inline object-parameter type literals in function signatures** — `function update(input: { id: string; name?: string })`, never a standalone `type UpdateInput = { … }` alias readers must scroll to resolve. Inlining keeps the contract at the call site, even with 5+ fields; `Deps<typeof fn>` / `Parameters<typeof fn>` extract from the function itself, so tests don't break. Don't refactor pre-existing aliases unless asked.
- **A reviewer's "why" goes in the PR body or the branch description, never a code comment**; a `/** */` block above an import or a const is not JSDoc.
- **A new finite-value field is a `String` column with `@default("…")`, never a Prisma `enum`** — the values live in TypeScript (`const X = [...] as const`) and are enforced at boundaries (`z.enum(X)`); a text field changes without a migration or a table lock. Existing enums stay (#10549 added one).
